introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer FOUR questions in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and two outline maps of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown: 5. (a) Examine the dominant winds and their characteristics responsible for the seasons in Cameroon. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Cameroon lies between about 2 and 13 degrees N, so its seasons are controlled by the seasonal movement of the **Inter-Tropical Discontinuity (ITD)**, the zone where two air masses meet. Two dominant winds are involved.

| | South-West monsoon (tropical maritime air) | North-East trade wind or Harmattan (tropical continental air) |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | South Atlantic Ocean (high pressure of St Helena) | Sahara and the Sahara high pressure |
| Direction | From the south-west | From the north-east |
| Characteristics | Warm, **humid**, unstable, laden with moisture | **Hot by day, cool at night, very dry**, dusty |
| Effects | Rain (relief rain on the windward slopes, convectional rain), cloud, high humidity | Dry weather, haze from dust, low humidity, drought, bush fires |
| Season | Rainy season | Dry season |

**How they cause the seasons.**
- **The ITD moves north** after March following the overhead sun (it reaches its most northerly position about July or August) and **south** after September (it is far to the south in about January). Where the south-west monsoon covers a place the weather is rainy; where the Harmattan covers it, it is dry.
- **South (equatorial regime).** The ITD passes twice, northwards and southwards, so there are **two rainy seasons** (about mid-March to June and September to mid-November) and two dry seasons (the long one from about December to February and the short one in July and August).
- **Centre, West and Adamawa.** The monsoon stays longer, giving **one long rainy season** (about March or April to October) and a short dry season.
- **North (tropical regime).** The monsoon arrives late and leaves early, giving **one short rainy season** (about May to October) and a **long dry season** (November to April) under the Harmattan.
- **Relief effect.** Mount Cameroon and the highlands force the moist monsoon to rise, so that the coast and the windward slopes receive very heavy rain (among the wettest places in Africa).

A sketch map on the outline map showing the arrows of the two winds and the position of the ITD in January and in July gains marks.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Show how wildlife constitutes one of the most important resources of the tourist industry in Cameroon. (7 marks)

(ii) Advance at least **four** reasons why Cameroon is yet to become an important tourist destination in Africa despite her rich tourist endowments. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(b)(i) Wildlife as a tourist resource (7 marks).**
- **A rich and varied fauna in many ecosystems.** Cameroon is often called "Africa in miniature". The **savanna parks of the north** (Waza, Benoue, Bouba Njida, Faro) shelter elephants, lions, giraffes, hippopotamuses, antelopes and many birds; the **rainforest** of the south and east (Dja Faunal Reserve, Lobeke, Campo-Ma'an, Korup in the South West) has forest elephants, gorillas, chimpanzees, drills, forest buffalo and many species of birds, butterflies and reptiles; the coast and the rivers have manatees, turtles and fish.
- **Protected areas.** National parks, reserves and sanctuaries (for example Waza National Park, the Limbe Wildlife Centre and the Mefou primate sanctuary) are the main attractions for photo-safaris, game viewing, bird watching, research and ecotourism; some, such as the Dja, are recognised as World Heritage sites.
- **Economic benefits.** Entrance and licence fees, safari and hunting concessions, hotels and guides provide foreign exchange and government revenue, **jobs** for guides, rangers and craftsmen, and income for the communities around the parks (a share of the revenue and sales of crafts and food).
- **Spin-off effects.** Wildlife tourism encourages roads, lodges and airstrips, develops local trade and raises awareness of **conservation**.
- **Seasonality.** The dry season (about November to April) is the best time for game viewing in the savanna parks, concentrating visitors in a period when farming is quiet.

**(b)(ii) Why Cameroon is not yet an important destination (any four, 8 marks).**
1. **Poor transport and infrastructure.** Roads to the parks, especially in the rainy season, are poor, air links are limited and internal flights costly, and parks lack good facilities.
2. **Inadequate accommodation and services** of an international standard outside the main towns, and a shortage of trained guides and tourism staff.
3. **Insecurity.** Attacks by armed groups in the Far North and the crisis in the English-speaking regions, and cross-border insecurity, discourage visitors; this also affects the image of the country.
4. **Weak marketing and publicity.** Cameroon is little known internationally as a destination and spends little on promotion compared with East and Southern Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa).
5. **Cumbersome entry procedures and high costs**: visa formalities, high air fares and hotel prices, and administrative delays.
6. **Poaching and habitat loss**, which reduce the animals to be seen, and weak management of parks.
7. **Insufficient investment and policy support** from the state and the private sector, and health risks (malaria and other diseases) that visitors fear.
8. **Competition** from better organised destinations elsewhere in Africa.
